unit.title: Other assets
unit.description: SOCIMIs, derivatives, CFDs, pension plans and where to keep short-term money

u11l1.title: Property on the stock market: SOCIMIs and REITs

steps.title: Property without buying a flat
steps.body:
A **SOCIMI** (in Spain) or a **REIT** (in the US and other countries) is a listed company that owns rental properties: offices, shopping centres, logistics warehouses, homes…

You buy its shares on the stock market like any other and become the owner of a slice of those buildings.

steps.title: The rules of the game
steps.body:
In exchange for paying very little corporation tax, they must **pay out most of their profit**: a SOCIMI, at least **80 %** of what comes from rents; a US REIT, at least **90 %** of its taxable profit.

That's why they usually pay high dividends.

steps.title: Pros and risks
steps.body: Pros: you diversify across many properties with little money and can sell in seconds. Risks: they're listed and **can fall like the stock market**, they suffer when rates rise (they borrow and compete with bonds) and they depend on their sector, like offices after the pandemic.
steps.key: A SOCIMI is bricks and mortar that trades on the market: diversified and liquid, but with stock-market volatility.
steps.tip: Buying a flat isn't the only way to invest in property.

u11l2.title: Futures and options in one lesson

steps.title: Futures
steps.body:
A **future** is a contract to buy or sell something on a **future date** at a **price agreed today**. Both sides are **obliged** to go through with it.

It's used to hedge (a farmer locks in the price of their wheat today) or to speculate. You only put down **margin**, a fraction of the value: that's **leverage**.

steps.title: Options
steps.body:
An **option** gives you the **right, but not the obligation**, to buy (**call**) or sell (**put**) at an agreed price (the **strike**) up to a certain date. For that right you pay a **premium**.

If it doesn't suit you, you let it expire and lose the premium. Whoever sells it collects the premium and takes on the obligation.

steps.title: Why they're not for beginners
steps.body: They're **derivatives**: their value depends on another asset. With leverage, a small move turns into a big gain or loss, and in some cases (selling options, futures) you can lose more than you put in.
steps.key: Future = an obligation at an agreed price. Option = a right in exchange for a premium.
steps.tip: If you can't explain how much you could lose in the worst case, don't trade derivatives.

steps.title: What a CFD is
steps.body:
A **CFD** (contract for difference) is a contract with your broker to receive or pay the **price difference** of an asset between when you open and close the trade. You don't buy the asset: you bet on whether it goes up or down.

It's traded **with leverage**: you put down margin and control a much bigger position. And you pay **financing** for every night you keep it open.

steps.title: The maths of leverage
steps.body:
With €1,000 and 20 to 1 leverage, you control **€20,000**. If the asset drops 5 %, you lose €1,000: **all your margin**.

In the EU, the maximum for retail investors is 30 to 1 on major currencies, 20 to 1 on major indices and gold, 5 to 1 on shares and **2 to 1 on crypto**.

steps.title: The CNMV's mandatory warning
steps.body: «CFDs are complex instruments and come with a high risk of losing money rapidly due to leverage. **Between 74 and 89 % of retail investor accounts lose money when trading CFDs.**» Each broker must also display its own percentage.
steps.key: Leverage multiplies gains and, above all, losses: most retail investors lose money with CFDs.
steps.tip: If a CFD ad hides the risk warning, be twice as suspicious.

steps.title: Tax relief today, tax tomorrow
steps.body:
What you pay into a **pension plan** reduces your taxable income for IRPF (Spanish income tax): up to **€1,500 a year** in a personal plan, which can be raised with employer contributions (workplace plans) up to **€10,000** in total.

If your marginal rate is 30 %, paying in €1,500 saves you **€450** of IRPF that year.

steps.title: The small print
steps.body:
• When you cash it in, **everything** (contributions and gains) is taxed as **employment income**, at your marginal rate at that time.
• **Limited access:** you can only cash it in at retirement or in specific cases (long-term unemployment, serious illness, disability, dependency), or contributions that are more than **10 years** old.
• Many bank plans charge high fees.

steps.title: When it makes sense
steps.body: It pays off mainly if your marginal rate today is **high**, you expect it to be **lower** when you retire and you won't need that money. For someone starting work on a low salary, the advantage is small.
steps.key: A pension plan defers tax and locks your money away: useful if you pay a lot of IRPF today.
steps.tip: What a pension plan doesn't save you is fees: check them.

u11l5.title: Deposits, savings accounts and money market funds

steps.title: Three places for the short term
steps.body:
• **Interest-bearing account:** pays interest and you can take your money out whenever you like. Watch out for limits: sometimes it only pays on up to a certain amount or for a few months.
• **Fixed-term deposit:** you lock your money away for a while at a fixed rate.
• **Money market fund:** invests in very short-term, high-quality debt. Its return follows ECB rates.

steps.title: What protects each one
steps.body:
Accounts and deposits are covered by the **Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos** (Spain's deposit guarantee scheme) up to **€100,000** per holder and per bank.

The money market fund **isn't** covered by that scheme, but its assets belong to the unitholders and are kept separate from the management company; its risk is very low, not zero. And, as a fund, it can be **transferred** without paying tax.

steps.title: What they're for
steps.body: For your **emergency fund** and money you'll need within months or a few years. Always compare the **APR** and the terms. None of the three is for the long term: after tax and inflation, they barely gain any purchasing power.
steps.key: Short term: access and safety before returns.
steps.tip: An emergency fund isn't there to earn: it's there to be there when you need it.

options: A listed company that invests in rental properties
u11l1-1.explanation: It's the Spanish version of a REIT: rental properties inside a listed company.

u11l1-2.prompt: Match each concept to its meaning.
u11l1-2.explanation: Property, payout rules and the advantage of being able to sell whenever you want.
right: Paying out most of the profit
Being able to sell on the market in seconds

u11l1-3.prompt: A SOCIMI makes 10 million in profit from rents. What's the minimum it must pay out as dividends?

u11l1-4.prompt: A SOCIMI trades at €10 and pays out €0.45 a year. What is its dividend yield?

u11l1-5.prompt: SOCIMIs can't fall much in price because they have buildings behind them.
u11l1-5.explanation: They're listed on the stock market: in a crisis or when rates rise they can fall a lot, like other shares.

u11l1-6.prompt: With a SOCIMI you can invest in property with far less money than buying a flat.
u11l1-6.explanation: All it takes is buying a few shares on the stock market.

u11l1-7.prompt: Your own buy-to-let flat or a SOCIMI?
options: You find the tenant and fix the boiler
Its price changes every day on the market
You need tens of thousands of euros as a deposit
u11l1-7.explanation: A SOCIMI gives you liquidity and diversification; your own flat, full control, but a lot of money in one place and plenty of work.

u11l1-8.prompt: Interest rates rise sharply and SOCIMIs fall 25 %. Bruno, who owns a few, panics. What should he bear in mind?
options: That the government will pay back his loss
That listed property companies are sensitive to rates and that this is part of their risk
That this shouldn't happen with property
u11l1-8.explanation: Knowing an asset's risks in advance helps you not to react in the heat of the moment when they show up.
feedback: Nobody guarantees the price of a share.
Good: if he knew this when he bought, he can decide based on his plan, not on the scare.
It does happen: they borrow to buy and, with high rates, borrowing costs more and bonds compete with their dividends.

u11l1-9.prompt: Quick: what's the minimum share of its rental profit a SOCIMI must pay out?
u11l1-9.explanation: It's one of the conditions for its special tax regime.

u11l1-10.prompt: What are the risks of investing in a SOCIMI? Select all.
options: Its sector doing badly (empty offices, for example)
Its price falling with the stock market
u11l1-10.explanation: The SOCIMI manages the properties; you take on market, interest-rate and sector risks.

u11l2-1.prompt: Match each term to its definition.
u11l2-1.explanation: The key difference: a future obliges you; a bought option only gives you a right.
right: Right to sell at an agreed price
What you pay for an option
Right to buy at an agreed price
Obligation to buy or sell on a date at an agreed price

u11l2-2.prompt: An option gives you the ____, but not the obligation, to buy or sell.
u11l2-2.explanation: That's why the buyer pays a premium: they're free not to use it.

u11l2-3.prompt: An option to buy is called a ____.
u11l2-3.explanation: A put is the option to sell; the strike is the agreed price.

u11l2-4.prompt: You buy a call with a strike of €100 and pay a €5 premium. At expiry the share is worth €112. How much do you make per share?
u11l2-4.explanation: You buy for €100 something worth €112: €12 − €5 premium = €7.

u11l2-5.prompt: With the same call (strike €100, premium €5), at expiry the share is worth €95. How much do you lose per share?
u11l2-5.explanation: There's no point buying for €100 something worth €95: you don't exercise it and you lose the premium, €5.

u11l2-6.prompt: A farmer is worried the price of wheat will fall before the harvest. What use of futures makes sense for them?
options: Sell futures today to lock in the price they'll get for their wheat
Do nothing: futures are only for speculating
Buy wheat futures to make more if it rises
u11l2-6.explanation: Derivatives can reduce a risk you already have (hedging) or create a new one (speculation).
feedback: Good: that's a hedge. If the price falls, the future makes up for it; if it rises, they give up that gain.
They were invented precisely to hedge risks like this one.
That doubles their bet that wheat will rise, the exact opposite of hedging.

u11l2-7.prompt: Marta sees someone on social media who «makes thousands a month selling options» and wants to try it with her savings. What should she bear in mind?
options: That selling options is collecting easy premiums with no risk
That by selling options she can lose far more than she collects, and that she should understand it first without real money
That if it's on social media, it's been proven
u11l2-7.explanation: Whoever sells an option collects a little and takes on a risk that can be huge.
feedback: You collect small premiums many times… until a sharp move makes you lose far more than you've taken in.
Good: selling a call without owning the share has, in theory, unlimited losses.
Social media shows the gains, rarely the losses.

u11l2-8.prompt: With a bought option, the most you can lose is the premium.
u11l2-8.explanation: If exercising it doesn't suit you, you let it expire: you lose what you paid and nothing more.

u11l2-9.prompt: Quick: which kind of option gives you the right to sell?

u11l2-10.prompt: Do they have an obligation or just a right?
options: Seller of an option, if the buyer exercises it
u11l2-10.explanation: With a future, both sides are bound; with an option, the buyer has the right and the seller, the obligation.

u11l3-1.prompt: You put down €1,000 of margin with 20 to 1 leverage. What position size do you control?

u11l3-2.prompt: With that €20,000 position, the asset falls 2 %. How much do you lose?
u11l3-2.explanation: 20,000 × 2 % = €400: 40 % of your margin from a 2 % move.

u11l3-3.prompt: With 20 to 1 leverage, what fall in the asset wipes out all your margin?
u11l3-3.explanation: 100 % ÷ 20 = 5 %. A normal move over a few weeks can wipe it out.

u11l3-4.prompt: According to the CNMV's mandatory warning, between 74 and 89 % of retail investors lose money with CFDs.
u11l3-4.explanation: It's the figure from ESMA's 2018 intervention, which every broker must display alongside its own percentage.

u11l3-5.prompt: With a CFD on a share, you own that share.
u11l3-5.explanation: You just have a contract with the broker on the price difference: no ownership and no vote.

u11l3-6.prompt: In the EU, a retail investor can trade crypto CFDs with 100 to 1 leverage.
u11l3-6.explanation: The maximum for retail investors on crypto is 2 to 1.

u11l3-7.prompt: Select the messages that are a warning sign or a scam.
options: «I'm your personal account manager. Deposit €250 and I'll trade for you with 1:500 leverage.»
«Copy my CFD trades: 95 % win rate guaranteed.»
«Multiply your money x50 with gold CFDs. No risk. Limited places.»
«Warning: between 74 and 89 % of retail investor accounts lose money with CFDs.»
u11l3-7.explanation: Returns «with no risk», leverage banned for retail investors in the EU, «account managers» who message you and guaranteed wins are classic signs of an unauthorised firm.

u11l3-8.prompt: Why do most retail investors lose money with CFDs?
options: Leverage turns small moves into big losses, and there are costs every night on top
Because they can only be traded in the early hours
u11l3-8.explanation: Leverage, financing costs and heat-of-the-moment decisions: a combination that hits beginners hardest.

u11l3-9.prompt: Quick: 10 to 1 leverage and the asset falls 3 %. What share of your margin do you lose?

u11l3-10.prompt: Pablo opened a leveraged CFD and he's losing. The broker warns him that his margin has fallen to half of what's required. What happens if it keeps falling?
options: The broker gives him back the money he lost
The broker closes the position and he can't lose more than he has in the account
Nothing, the broker waits for it to recover
u11l3-10.explanation: European rules limit the damage (close-out at 50 % and no negative balance), but they don't stop you losing what you deposited.
feedback: Exactly: retail investors get automatic close-out and negative balance protection, but the loss is already his.
No: in the EU, when margin falls to 50 % of what's required, the broker closes the position and the loss becomes real.

u11l4-1.prompt: Your marginal IRPF (Spanish income tax) rate is 30 % and you pay €1,500 into your personal plan. How much IRPF do you save that year?

u11l4-2.prompt: With a marginal rate of 19 %, how much do you save by paying in €1,500?
u11l4-2.explanation: 1,500 × 19 % = €285. The lower your rate, the smaller the advantage.

u11l4-3.prompt: How is cashing in a pension plan taxed?
options: As savings income, only on the gain
As employment income, at your marginal rate, on everything you cash in
u11l4-3.explanation: Since contributions got tax relief on the way in, everything is taxed on the way out.

u11l4-4.prompt: What is the general contribution limit for a personal pension plan?
u11l4-4.explanation: You can reach €10,000 in total only by adding contributions to workplace plans.

u11l4-5.prompt: When can you cash in a pension plan? Select all.
options: Contributions that are more than 10 years old
Whenever you like, to go on holiday
u11l4-5.explanation: Outside those cases, the money is locked away.

u11l4-6.prompt: Ana is 23, earns little and her marginal rate is low. Her bank offers her a plan with a 1.5 % annual fee «for the tax relief». What should she bear in mind?
options: That the advantage depends on her marginal rate, the fees and her not needing the money
That she won't pay tax when she cashes it in
That tax relief always pays off
u11l4-6.explanation: A pension plan isn't good or bad in general: it depends on your marginal rate, its costs and your time horizon.
feedback: Good: it pays off more with high rates today, low fees and money you won't need.
She will: everything she cashes in is taxed as employment income.
With a low rate the tax advantage is small, and the money is locked away for decades paying 1.5 % a year.

u11l4-7.prompt: When you cash in a pension plan you only pay tax on the gains, not on what you paid in.
u11l4-7.explanation: Everything is taxed, contributions and gains, because the contributions already got tax relief.

u11l4-8.prompt: Contributions to a pension plan reduce your taxable income for IRPF.
u11l4-8.explanation: Up to the limit of €1,500 a year in a personal plan.

u11l4-9.prompt: Put the life of a pension plan in order.
options: The money is invested for years without being taxed
Retirement or another cash-in event arrives
You cash it in and it's taxed as employment income
You pay in and reduce your IRPF that year
u11l4-9.explanation: You get tax relief going in, the money grows untaxed and you pay on the way out.

u11l4-10.prompt: Advantage or drawback of a pension plan?
options: When you cash it in, everything is taxed as employment income
Gains aren't taxed while it stays invested
High fees on many bank plans
Reduces your IRPF in the year you pay in
u11l4-10.explanation: Weigh up both columns before deciding; which way it tips depends on your situation.

u11l5-1.prompt: Match each product to its feature.
u11l5-1.explanation: Three products for the short term and the safety net that covers two of them.
right: Money locked away at a fixed rate
Covers up to €100,000 per holder and per bank
Very short-term debt; can be transferred

u11l5-2.prompt: You have €6,000 in an account at 2 % APR for a year. How much gross interest do you earn?

u11l5-3.prompt: An account pays 3 % APR, but only on the first €5,000; the rest earns 0 %. You have €8,000. Gross interest over a year?
u11l5-3.explanation: 5,000 × 3 % = €150; the other €3,000 earn nothing. On €8,000, that's 1.875 %.

u11l5-4.prompt: A deposit pays 2.5 % and inflation is 2.7 %. Approximate real return before tax?
u11l5-4.explanation: 2.5 − 2.7 = −0.2 %: it doesn't even keep up your purchasing power.

u11l5-5.prompt: Which of these products is NOT covered by Spain's deposit guarantee scheme (FGD)?
u11l5-5.explanation: The FGD covers deposits; a money market fund is an investment fund, with its assets kept separate from the management company.

u11l5-6.explanation: The FGD covers money deposited in banks, not investments in funds or shares.

u11l5-7.prompt: Bruno wants a €6,000 emergency fund. He's torn between a 3-year deposit with an early-withdrawal penalty, an interest-bearing account with no lock-in and an equity ETF. What suits an emergency fund best?
options: The equity ETF, which returns more over the long run
The interest-bearing account with no lock-in
The 3-year deposit, which pays a bit more
u11l5-7.explanation: An emergency fund has to be available and not depend on the stock market.
feedback: In a crisis it could fall 30 % just when he needs it most.
Good: available instantly, covered by the FGD and with some interest.
If an emergency comes up, cancelling it will cost him the penalty.

u11l5-8.prompt: Quick: what does the APR measure?
u11l5-8.explanation: It lets you compare products with different terms and payment schedules.

u11l5-9.prompt: In Spain, a money market fund can be transferred to another fund without paying tax.
u11l5-9.explanation: It's an investment fund, so it has the transfer regime.

u11l5-10.prompt: A money market fund can never lose money.
u11l5-10.explanation: Its risk is very low, not zero: it invests in debt that, in extreme cases, can fall in price or not be repaid.
